````math
## Appendix D Experimental Setup

### D.1 Comparison Baselines

We compare CasePlay against two groups of baselines: *existing medical
reasoning models* and *state-of-the-art self-play methods*. For medical
reasoning models, we select three representative models, including:

- •
  HuatuoGPT-o1 \[[2](#bib.bib1)\] is among the first works to study how
  to improve medical reasoning through RL. It first uses SFT to elicit
  medical reasoning behavior and then applies RL with medical verifiable
  rewards to enhance reasoning performance.
- •
  AlphaMed \[[30](#bib.bib6)\] systematically studies how minimalist
  rule-based RL can improve model performance on medical reasoning
  benchmarks. It further highlights the importance of training data
  diversity for enhancing medical reasoning ability, making it a strong
  representative of medical RL post-training.
- •
  Fleming-R1 \[[31](#bib.bib3)\] follows an offline data construction
  pipeline that first builds medical knowledge graphs and then
  synthesizes QA questions from the constructed graphs. The synthesized
  QA data are then used for RL training, leading to strong performance
  among medical reasoning models.

For self-play methods, we include one document-free self-play baseline
and two recent document-grounded self-play baselines:

- •
  R-Zero \[[14](#bib.bib42)\]: R-Zero is a zero-data self-play framework
  in which a proposer generates questions based on its own internal
  knowledge, and a reasoner learns from the generated questions. We
  include this baseline to examine whether self-play that relies only on
  the model’s internal knowledge is sufficient for medical reasoning. In
  our implementation, we remove both document input and knowledge-point
  conditioning from the proposer, and also remove rubric-judge feedback.
  All other training details follow the original R-Zero setup as closely
  as possible under our backbone model and training budget.
- •
  SPICE \[[17](#bib.bib43)\]: SPICE is a document-grounded self-play
  method that uses unlabeled text to support challenger question
  generation. Unlike CasePlay, SPICE uses the same model as both
  proposer and reasoner, and updates them jointly within each batch.
  Following SPICE, we merge proposer-side and reasoner-side data for
  warm-start training, and then jointly sample and update the shared
  model during self-play. We keep the number of update examples matched
  to CasePlay for a fair comparison.
- •
  DARC \[[18](#bib.bib44)\]: DARC is a two-stage document-grounded
  self-play method that trains the challenger and reasoner separately.
  Following its original design, we first train the proposer with
  explicit difficulty targets using grounding and difficulty rewards,
  and then use the trained proposer to generate questions for reasoner
  training. The total amount of training data is matched to CasePlay to
  ensure a fair comparison.

### D.2 Benchmarks

We evaluate CasePlay on 7 medically related benchmarks covering
expert-level medical reasoning, clinical case reasoning, and scientific
QA. All benchmarks are evaluated in a multiple-choice format. During
evaluation, we prompt the model to place its final answer in \boxed{},
and use math-verify \[[58](#bib.bib12)\] to extract the boxed answer and
compare it with the ground-truth option. The details of each benchmark
are as follows.

- •
  MedXpert-QA \[[33](#bib.bib28)\] is an expert-level medical QA
  benchmark designed to evaluate advanced clinical knowledge and
  reasoning. In this paper, we evaluate on the MedXpert-Text subset,
  which contains 2,450 text-only multiple-choice questions.
- •
  MedBullets-OP4/OP5 \[[34](#bib.bib29)\] consists of exam-style medical
  questions derived from MedBullets. We evaluate both the four-option
  and five-option variants, denoted as OP4 and OP5, respectively. Each
  variant contains 308 questions.
- •
  MedQA-USMLE \[[35](#bib.bib4)\] is a widely used medical exam
  benchmark collected from United States Medical Licensing
  Examination-style questions, evaluating a model’s ability to apply
  medical knowledge and clinical reasoning in realistic clinical
  scenarios. We use the standard test split, which contains 1,273
  questions.
- •
  LiveClin \[[25](#bib.bib27)\] is a clinical case reasoning benchmark
  built from patient-centered clinical scenarios. It emphasizes
  realistic case-based reasoning, including symptom interpretation,
  diagnosis, and treatment decision-making. Since the original benchmark
  contains multimodal questions, we filter out questions that depend on
  figures or images, resulting in 1,450 text-only questions.
- •
  MMLU-Pro \[[36](#bib.bib18)\] is a challenging extension of MMLU with
  harder questions and expanded answer choices. We evaluate the
  medically related Biology and Health subsets, which contain 717 and
  818 questions, respectively, for a total of 1,535 questions.
- •
  GPQA \[[37](#bib.bib17)\] consists of graduate-level scientific QA
  questions designed to test expert-level scientific reasoning. We
  evaluate the medically related Genetics and Molecular Biology subsets,
  which contain 20 and 83 questions, respectively, for a total of 103
  questions.

### D.3 Training Setup and Hyperparameters

Our implementation is built on Verl \[[59](#bib.bib11)\] and
vLLM \[[60](#bib.bib16)\]. Since proposer and reasoner rollouts are
executed alternately, we disable GPU colocation in Verl and use
Ray \[[61](#bib.bib55)\] to repartition computational resources. Our
final setup uses six 8-GPU nodes, with GPUs allocated to the proposer
and reasoner in a 2:4 ratio, which yields the best runtime performance
in our experiments.

Before self-play, we construct a small warm-start dataset as described
in
Section [C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 Data Preparation ‣ Appendix C Implementation Details ‣ CasePlay: Self-Play Reinforcement Learning from Case Reports for Medical Reasoning").
For fair comparison, all self-play methods use this same warm-start
dataset for initialization. We warm-start the proposer and reasoner
separately for 5 epochs with learning rate $`1\times 10^{-5}`$. For
self-play RL, we optimize the proposer and reasoner alternately with
GRPO for $`T=15`$ iterations. Each iteration contains $`U_{P}=10`$
proposer-update steps and $`U_{R}=10`$ reasoner-update steps. During
proposer rollouts, each document produces $`N_{p}=4`$ proposer
candidates, and each candidate is answered by the reasoner
$`N_{\mathrm{acc}}=4`$ times to estimate learnability. During reasoner
updates, we sample $`N_{r}=8`$ responses per selected question. Full
hyperparameters are listed in
Table [5](#A4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ D.3 Training Setup and Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix D Experimental Setup ‣ CasePlay: Self-Play Reinforcement Learning from Case Reports for Medical Reasoning").

|  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| SFT Warm-Start |  |  |  |  |  |
| Epochs | 5 | Batch size | 128 | Max response len. | 8,192 |
| Learning rate | $`1{\times}10^{-5}`$ | LR schedule | Cosine | LR warmup ratio | 0.1 |
| Self-Play RL |  |  |  |  |  |
| Optimization |  | Rollout |  | Others |  |
| Learning rate | $`1{\times}10^{-6}`$ | Proposer samples $`N_{p}`$ | 4 | Invalid penalty $`r^{\mathrm{format}}`$ | -0.1 |
| Train batch | 128 | Answer samples $`N_{\mathrm{acc}}`$ | 4 | Learnability weight | 1.0 |
| Proposer steps $`U_{P}`$ | 10 | Reasoner samples $`N_{r}`$ | 8 | Rubric weight $`\lambda`$ | 0.2 |
| Reasoner steps $`U_{R}`$ | 10 | Max input len. | 4,096 | Number of knowledge points $`M`$ | 4 |
| Clip upper | 0.28 | Max response len. | 8,192 |  |  |

#### Robustness of Performance Gains and Confidence Intervals.

Table [6](#A5.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Appendix E Additional Experimental Results ‣ CasePlay: Self-Play Reinforcement Learning from Case Reports for Medical Reasoning")
reports mean accuracies and standard deviations over three training
seeds. Each checkpoint is evaluated with eight responses per question
(24 across the three checkpoints); 95% CIs are estimated by percentile
bootstrapping over training runs and evaluation questions. CasePlay
achieves the highest mean accuracy on all seven benchmarks, with an
average accuracy of 66.2%, compared with 65.0% for DARC, 63.7% for
SPICE, and 62.4% for R-Zero. The reported confidence intervals for
CasePlay lie entirely above those for SPICE on MedQA and LiveClin, and
above those for R-Zero on MedXpert, MB-OP4, MedQA, LiveClin, and
MMLU-Pro. Although the intervals overlap in the remaining comparisons,
the consistent advantage in mean accuracy across all seven benchmarks
provides empirical support for the effectiveness of CasePlay in
improving medical reasoning under the three-run evaluation.

| Static Synthetic Data + GRPO | 22.6 | 75.0 | 69.5 | 84.1 | 66.9 | 75.6 | 55.3 | 64.1 |
| CasePlay | 25.1 | 76.9 | 70.1 | 85.4 | 72.3 | 75.9 | 57.6 | 66.2 |

#### Effectiveness of the Self-Play Training Paradigm.

To assess adaptive self-play relative to a fixed-data training pipeline,
we use DeepSeek-V3.2 \[[38](#bib.bib9)\] to generate approximately 19K
question–answer pairs from the same 4,281 case reports. This synthetic
pool remains fixed throughout GRPO training. We match the warm-start
reasoner, the number of training pairs, and the reasoner GRPO update
budget to CasePlay. As shown in
Table [7](#A5.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Robustness of Performance Gains and Confidence Intervals. ‣ Appendix E Additional Experimental Results ‣ CasePlay: Self-Play Reinforcement Learning from Case Reports for Medical Reasoning"),
CasePlay outperforms the static baseline on all seven benchmarks,
achieving an average accuracy of 66.2% versus 64.1%. This comparison
supports the effectiveness of adaptive self-play under the matched
reasoner update budget. A plausible explanation is that adapting
question generation to the evolving reasoner helps maintain informative
response groups: questions that elicit uniformly correct or incorrect
responses provide no correctness-driven group-relative learning signal
under binary rewards.

| Fleming-R1-7B | 19.1 | 57.8 | 54.1 | 75.1 | 60.2 | 69.3 | 48.7 | 54.9 |
| $`+`$ CasePlay | 20.2 | 61.6 | 57.9 | 76.5 | 65.3 | 69.6 | 50.2 | 57.3 |

#### Compatibility with Medical RL Post-Training.

We next investigate whether CasePlay can further improve a reasoner that
has already undergone medical RL post-training. We initialize the
reasoner from Fleming-R1-7B \[[31](#bib.bib3)\] and continue training
with CasePlay on the clinical case-report corpus, using the same Avg@8
evaluation protocol. As shown in
Table [8](#A5.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Effectiveness of the Self-Play Training Paradigm. ‣ Appendix E Additional Experimental Results ‣ CasePlay: Self-Play Reinforcement Learning from Case Reports for Medical Reasoning"),
average accuracy increases from 54.9% to 57.3%, a gain of 2.4 percentage
points. Performance improves on all seven benchmarks, with the largest
gain on LiveClin, from 60.2% to 65.3% (+5.1 percentage points). This
continuation experiment shows that CasePlay provides additional gains
for the evaluated medical RL model, supporting its use as a subsequent
training stage after medical RL post-training.

#### Quality Analysis of Generated Questions.

We next examine how the rubric scores of generated questions evolve
during training.
Figure [8](#A5.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ Quality Analysis of Generated Questions. ‣ Appendix E Additional Experimental Results ‣ CasePlay: Self-Play Reinforcement Learning from Case Reports for Medical Reasoning")
compares the three rubric scores throughout training with and without
rubric-based feedback. Incorporating this feedback improves all three
dimensions, with the most pronounced gains in clue integration and
reasoning depth. This pattern suggests that the rubric encourages the
proposer to construct questions requiring the integration of multiple
clinical clues and multistep reasoning, extending the training signal
beyond estimated difficulty. Improvements in option quality are more
modest. One plausible explanation is that constructing discriminative
distractors depends more heavily on the proposer’s parametric medical
knowledge, while clue integration and reasoning depth can be influenced
more directly through the selection and composition of case evidence.
The variant without rubric feedback also improves at some stages, but
its scores remain lower and less stable. These results indicate that
learnability-based feedback alone provides weaker control over the
quality of generated questions.

#### Impact of Knowledge-point Selection Strategy.

We compare three strategies for selecting knowledge points during
question generation: *random*, *round-robin*, and *accuracy-priority*.
For a document $`d`$ with extracted knowledge points
$`K(d)=\{k_{1},\ldots,k_{M}\}`$, the *random* strategy uniformly samples
one knowledge point from $`K(d)`$ at each rollout. The *round-robin*
strategy selects knowledge points cyclically, as described in
Eq. ([4](#S3.E4 "Equation 4 ‣ Knowledge-Conditioned Question Generation. ‣ 3.1 Knowledge-Conditioned Proposer ‣ 3 Proposed Solution: CasePlay ‣ CasePlay: Self-Play Reinforcement Learning from Case Reports for Medical Reasoning")).
The *accuracy-priority* strategy samples knowledge points according to
the current reasoner’s average answer accuracy on questions generated
from each knowledge point. Specifically, for knowledge point $`k_{m}`$,
its sampling probability is defined by applying a softmax over the
learnability scores,
$`p(k_{m}\mid d)=\mathrm{softmax}_{k_{m}\in K(d)}(1-2|\bar{a}_{m}-0.5|)`$,
where $`\bar{a}_{m}`$ is the current reasoner’s average accuracy on
questions associated with $`k_{m}`$.

| Strategy      | DCR $`\uparrow`$ | Avg. Acc. $`\uparrow`$ |
|---------------|------------------|------------------------|
| Random        | 0.40             | 65.7                   |
| Acc.-priority | 0.32             | 64.1                   |
| Round-robin   | 0.42             | 66.2                   |

Table 9: Impact of knowledge-point selection strategies.

As shown in
Table [9](#A5.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Impact of Knowledge-point Selection Strategy. ‣ Appendix E Additional Experimental Results ‣ CasePlay: Self-Play Reinforcement Learning from Case Reports for Medical Reasoning"),
*round-robin* achieves the best performance, with the highest document
coverage ratio (0.42) and the highest average accuracy (66.2). The
*random* strategy is competitive, but its stochastic selection can
repeatedly sample the same knowledge points, leading to slightly lower
coverage and downstream performance. In contrast, *accuracy-priority*
substantially reduces document coverage (0.32) and achieves the lowest
average accuracy. Since each document is sampled only a limited number
of times during self-play, prioritizing knowledge points based on noisy
intermediate accuracy estimates can over-concentrate generation on a
small subset of knowledge points, reducing within-document diversity and
weakening the effectiveness of self-play RL. We therefore adopt
*round-robin* as the default strategy in CasePlay.

## Appendix F Limitations

Despite the strong empirical gains of CasePlay, our current
implementation extracts a fixed set of knowledge points before self-play
training and keeps them unchanged throughout RL. This design provides a
stable and controllable basis for knowledge-conditioned generation,
which helps reduce redundant question generation and improve training
efficiency. However, it also limits the framework’s ability to adapt its
knowledge-point coverage as the proposer and reasoner improve. Future
work could explore online discovery, pruning, and refinement of
knowledge points when learning from unlabeled medical corpora.
Additionally, our experiments focus on text-grounded case reports and
text-only benchmark settings, while many medical corpora contain images
that provide important clinical evidence. Extending CasePlay to
multimodal self-play is therefore an important direction for improving
its practical utility in medical reasoning. Such an extension could
allow the framework to generate and evaluate questions grounded in both
textual and visual evidence, making self-play learning better aligned
with real clinical case reasoning.

## Appendix G Broader Impacts

This work aims to improve medical reasoning models by learning from
unlabeled clinical case reports. Potential benefits include reducing
reliance on costly expert annotations and supporting research on medical
education and clinical question answering. However, the work also has
risks. Models trained with this framework may produce incorrect or
overconfident medical answers, and case reports may contain biases
because they often describe unusual or publication-worthy cases rather
than representative patient populations. There are also privacy concerns
when using medical text, even if the data are publicly available, and
stronger medical reasoning models could be misused to generate
misleading health information. We view CasePlay as a research framework,
not a deployable clinical decision-making system. Any downstream use
should require de-identified and properly licensed data, careful
factuality and bias evaluation, clear communication of limitations, and
human clinical oversight.
````
